speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler), of which I have given him notice, based partly on an item which I read in the Ottawa Journal this morning, as follows:
Washington, March 7.-Discussions with Canada have begun in an effort to iron out a number of difficulties that arose after the new trade agreement with the dominion went into effect January 1.
In view of these discussions I wish to draw to the attention of the minister the very acute and urgent situation in which Ontario wheat farmers find themselves, due to the fact that they are finding it impossible to sell their wheat through the usual channels while at the same time they claim that over 600,000 bushels of subsidized American wheat have been brought into Ontario to be used by certain Ontario flour mills. It is claimed that one of these users of subsidized American wheat is offering flour at $2.60 per barrel 
in Montreal, whereas flour made from Ontario soft winter wheat could not to-day be sold for less than $2.90 per barrel. That is the statement to me, and I should like to ask the minister if this matter will be discussed with the committee which is referred to in the newspaper item I have quoted.
Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce); Mr. Speaker, while the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) did give me notice that he intended to ask this question, I had not seen the article and he did not read it to me in detail. However, for his information and the information of the house I might say that so far as a United States committee discussing matters with the Canadian government is concerned, I have no knowledge of any such committee meeting any representatives of the Canadian government, and I think I should know if such a conference were taking place.
With regard to the importation of United States wheat by mills in Ontario, I have had considerable correspondence, including a good many letters from farmers and others in Ontario, complaining about the importations. There is no doubt that some wheat is coming in from the United States and being milled in Ontario, and possibly some of it is being exported. Perhaps this part of the question should be answered by my colleague the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley), but these importations are coming in under the law as it stands. I may admit, however, that the situation is giving some concern to the government, but at the moment I can only say that it is receiving consideration.

Mr. Speaker, just before the adjournment of this debate the other day I stated that the trouble with world trade was that every nation was trying to sell but those who wanted to buy found themselves short of purchasing power. That fact was recognized by the world conference of agricultural economists, who maintained that there was a chronic shortage of purchasing power throughout the world while on the other hand there was a tremendous surplus of commodities of all kinds. This holds true in this country as well, and I have suggested that we should increase the purchasing power of the consumer. Out of our wheat fields comes the wheat, but what do the farmers receive for it? Let me refer to some statements made by elevator agents in respect to the harvesting of the last crop:
"There is more than one farmer in this particular district wrho would be wiped out completely if called upon to satisfy all his creditors. However, I can't imagine his creditors adopting such a short-sighted policy. A number of them have threatened to turn back large portions of their farm lands if they are not given an opportunity to realize something on their crop this year. I know of one farmer who is actually turning back a section and a half of land to the municipality rather than pay his tax arrears. This particular farmer owes something like $7,000 in tax arrears, and he figures that he would be much further ahead if he surrendered his land rather than attempt to pay off the majority of his arrears out of this year's crop."
Another elevator agent also pointed out that many farmers were required to purchase new farming machinery this year, and these payments will also have to be made out of this year's crop in addition to the other debts piled up against it. The agent said that while the bushelage in many districts will exceed that of last year, the price of wheat is greatly reduced from last year.
"In fact it is generally admitted that it will take two bushels of grain to realize the same amount of money received for one bushel last year," the agent said.

^ Mr. HUGHES CLEAVER (Halton): Mr. Speaker, after a few general remarks in regard to the treaty I should like to confine most of my observations to those parts of it which have to do particularly with the fruit and vegetable industry, because an important part of my constituency is interested in the production of fruit and vegetables. The Canada-United States and the Great Britain-United States trade agreements, in so far as they encourage a closer relationship and better understanding among these three great democracies, are admittedly highly beneficial to a world filled with misunderstanding and misgivings.
Our friends of the Conservative party are opposing the Canada-United States trade agreement solely upon the ground that, according to their contention, the price which we have paid for the agreement is too high. In plain words they say the Yankees are better traders than we are, and that we have been outwitted. Personally I have no such inferiority complex with regard to the three gentlemen who had most to do with the negotiation of the agreement. I refer to Mr. Hector McKinnon of the Department of Finance, Mr. Wilgress of the Department of Trade and Commerce and Mr. Robertson of the Department of External Affairs. For many months these men carried on continuous negotiations, and instead of expressing dissatisfaction with the results it is my opinion that parliament and the Canadian people owe those men a great debt of gratitude.
In my opinion, when viewed by actual performance instead of by politically tinged prophecies, the treaty will prove to be one of the greatest economic accomplishments in the history of this nation. In giving directions to our negotiators, and in accepting the responsibility for the final result, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his ministers have taken a leading part in anc have made a real contribution to the consolidation of the democratic peoples in the world to-day. It is my opinion that had it not been for the spirit which Canada showed in negotiating the 1935 agreement with the United States, the present agreement could not have been consummated. Even though we had not been able to negotiate a trade agreement as advantageous as is the new trade agreement, it is my firm belief that present-day world conditions demanded that closer economic relations should be formed between the great democracies at almost any cost. Fortunately for Canada, we were not called upon to make any serious concessions and we have received many important advantages. It

They now say that the 1935 treaty was lopsided. In 1936, when our exports to the United States exceeded our imports from that country by $41,000,000 and the balance was then decidedly in our favour, we did not hear anything at all about the treaty being lopsided. Again in 1937, when the balance was still substantially in our favour, we heard no criticism. But in 1938 the treaty suddenly becomes fraught with inequalities. Right at this point, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a suggestion: Canadian prosperity depends upon the prosperity of Canada's customer nations. So long as we have large surpluses of the field, the forest and the mine, just so long we must of necessity be a world-trading nation, whether we want to or not. It necessarily follows that just as soon as any of our customers run into hard times, we shall suffer as a result of their hard times, and for this reason I believe our system of taxation should be set up in such a way that, when hard times come, all groups of our people will bear their reasonable share of the depression according to their ability to bear it.
During the last great depression many of our people were compelled to use up their entire life-savings, and to-day are penniless, while many others of our people still have their large fortunes intact. From a truly democratic point of view this should not be permitted. Our people are reasonable and do not expect us to accomplish the impossible, and when hard times come I do not think anyone would complain if everyone shared the hard times according to his or her ability. I therefore urge that the major part of our revenues should be collected by way of income tax, because in this way taxation would be paid according to one's actual yearly receipts.
What about other calamities which were to befall us as a result of the 1935 trade agreement? Well, we still have our birthright, Lanark notwithstanding. The union jack is still flying over Canada, Hamilton West notwithstanding. And what about the agricultural implement business? I should now like to direct my remarks to the fruit and vegetable industry. First, a few remarks in regard to the size of the industry. The house may be surprised to learn that at the bureau of statistics there is no information available respecting the vegetable industry other than that contained in the 1931 census. This is an extremely unsatisfactory and unbusinesslike state of affairs, and I should like to impress upon the minister the urgent necessity of an up-to-date record in regard to this industry.
In 1931 the total production of vegetables was approximately $33,000,000. Those who have been closely in touch with this industry know what a spectacular increase in production has since taken place. In January of this year, Messrs. Davis and Ritchie presented to the Ontario Vegetable Growers Association at Hamilton a report in which they estimated that, exclusive of field crops of potatoes, Canada has 627.000 acres devoted to the production of vegetables, now producing annually $90,000,000 worth of vegetables. Doctor Hopper, of the Department of Agriculture, has prepared an estimate based upon the per capita consumption of vegetables at Ottawa and Toronto, where accurate figures are available, and his estimate of Canada's production of vegetables is $86,000,000. After carefully 
checking the figures and the deductions on which these estimates are based I am convinced that both of them will be found to be extremely conservative. In any event, it will be seen that production in this industry has nearly trebled in the last eight years. This great increase in volume has been brought about from several causes:
1.	Trucking facilities have brought into production thousands of acres of land which previously were not accessible to large markets.
2.	The medical profession has in recent years stressed the importance of fresh vegetables from a health point of view. Many of the important vitamins required in a properly balanced diet can be obtained only through the use of fresh vegetables.
3.	Many farmers who, prior to the depression. were raising only grain, cattle, dairy produce and hogs, started raising vegetables to enhance their incomes. This, in turn, depressed the price of vegetables and compelled vegetable growers to step up their production in order to survive. The combined result of all of these factors has been to increase the gross production from $33,000,000 in 1931 to about $90,000,000 in 1938.
In regard to tree fruits and small fruits an estimate arrived at in the same manner as that used by Doctor Hopper in regard to vegetables would place our total fruit production at about $60,000,000. This would make a total production of fruit and vegetables in Canada of about $150,000,000 annually.
Marketing facilities have not kept pace with this greatly increased production, and as a result we find wide price fluctuations which are detrimental to consumers and producers alike. We have reached a point. Mr. Speaker, where modem marketing facilities are urgently needed, and on behalf of the growers in my riding and throughout Canada I do wish to commend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for the steps which he has already taken to improve marketing facilities, and to urge upon him the necessity for adequate central markets in all large centres in this dominion. These markets would be self-liquidating as to cost. I do not know of any greater contribution that our Department of Agriculture could make at this time to this industry than the building of fruit and vegetable markets.
I should now like to give some information in regard to the amount of capital invested in this industry and also as to the cost of production in order that an accurate conclusion may be reached as to the valuable contribution which this industry makes to our national life.

On account of the scarcity of suitable lands and suitable locations for the production of fruits and vegetables, the first major problem which a grower faces is the original investment for land suitable for his operations. In the Burlington district land suitable for the growing of fruits and vegetables has under normal conditions in the past commanded a price varying from $800 to $1,000 an acre for the bare land without buildings. If we take a fifteen acre farm as perhaps the average size farm suitable for the purpose-and there are many of our growers raising vegetables, alone, on farms as small as five acres per farm-it will be seen that a capital outlay of at least $12,000 is involved. To this amount must be added the cost of suitable buildings, which will involve at least another $6,000. This total of $18,000 is still not the entire capital outlay required, because the grower also requires quite a large quantity of equipment to assist him in (a) the cultivation of the land, (b) producing and caring for plants, (c) combating all the different pests and plant blight diseases which the grower encounters, (d) packing, storage and marketing facilities. Mr. Speaker, I have followed pretty closely the debate that has taken place so far in regard to this trade agreement, and it appears to me that members of the government are experiencing difficulty in discovering any benefits to which they can point as being likely to accrue to Canada under this arrangement. Yesterday the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) referred to what he called the delay in connection with the consideration of this treaty, and compared the length of time taken to debate the British empire trade agreements with the time that has been devoted to this agreement. It should be pointed out that the debate on the empire trade agreements required a total of twenty-six parliamentary days while on the other hand only seven parliamentary days have been devoted thus far to the discussion of the Canada-United States agreement, and we are now on the eighth day. So it is evident that there has been nothing in the way of any hold-up or delay in the consideration of this agreement. I would also suggest that if we took into account the time occupied by hon. members on the government side during this debate, with all the quotations they have read, with each taking his full forty minutes, I think it will be found that the Conservative opposition have not taken up a great deal of the time of this house in undue criticism.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, it is up to the government to establish in what way this treaty will relieve unemployment. It has been stated by some hon. members that this agreement could be judged only with the passage of time. But I would direct attention to the fact that it is now four years since the 1935 agreement became effective, and the unemployment question is still with us to a very marked degree. I do not

and dispose of our goods, where we can profitably do so, in order that we may build up and develop our Canadian industry. I believe it is the duty of the government to assist our manufacturers of primary and secondary products in order to dispose of their products in the markets of the world, because through that medium we could give employment to thousands of Canadians.
While I do not advocate a policy of government subsidization of industry, I do feel it would be of material assistance if our government were to encourage a system designed more materially to assist our manufacturers, in order that they may be able to provide the much needed employment in Canada at the present time. The argument is often advanced that as a result of tariffs prevailing price levels are increased. To those who advance this argument I would ask: What does it matter if the prevailing prices of goods are high, if our people have not the money or means to purchase them? It would not matter if you could buy a gold brick for ten cents, if you had not the ten cents.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
If we do not give employment to our people through the efforts of our manufacturers, and through our industries, how are they going to have any money? If the men and women in the urban districts of our country find themselves unemployed, and without money or purchasing power, it is only natural that they cannot be purchasers of the products of our rural districts.
I believe it is also essential that our government should give more consideration to the diversification of industry in Canada, so that the production of commodities may be increased, and our manufacturers and industrialists may assist materially in creating a greater number of skilled workers. Unskilled men, who possess no particular qualifications to fit them for employment, are to-day unemployed, and many of these men might be trained for skilled labour. I am confident a policy of this type, if given leadership by the government, would have the effect of producing a higher standard of living among the people.
I would suggest further that if the government is sincere in their endeavour to do something for Canada, that is to provide employment, to build great Canadian industries in Canada rather than in the United States, and to increase the purchasing power of our people, then it is time they put their tariff

experts to work on a revision of the duty on manufactured goods coming into Canada, so as to place this country in a position to bargain with countries which are shipping goods into the markets of Canada at tariff rates below those which apply to manufactured goods in their markets. A policy of this kind, if sincerely and diligently followed, would provide our Canadian manufacturers with a means to compete with foreign manufacturers, and especially those of the United States.
I have already cited examples which indicated that, in many cases, the duties against Canadian goods going into the markets of the United States are over one hundred per cent greater than the duty we impose against United States goods coming into competition with those of our manufacturers.
I hold in my hand an ordinary room key of a large hotel in Canada, and on it I see the words "Made in the U.S.A." This is one of a large number of small articles imported from the United States, in the production of which there is considerable labour content. If Canadians insisted upon made-in-Canada goods, we would produce these commodities and thereby give employment to our industrial workers. I believe almost all members of the house have at some time or another been in the United States and have made purchases in that country, but I am sure that on very few occasions have they seen over there a manufactured commodity labelled "Made in Canada." While visiting in the United States I have looked for articles marked in that way, and have failed to find them. I believe if any hon. member had seen such articles he would remember them, because we know they are very scarce. I have made many purchases in the United States and I believe I have never bought an article in that country labelled "Made in Canada."
This is one of the points I should like to present in an effort to show that our tariffs are onesided. When we enter the shops in Canada we find all classes of manufactured articles labelled "Made in Japan," "Made in Yugoslavia," or "Made in UEA." I could go on enumerating the names of countries in which articles being sold over our counters are made. I maintain that to a great extent this is the cause of unemployment in Canada. If our manufacturers, through a fair tariff arrangement, had opportunities to sell their products in other countries, we should have prosperity and very little trouble with hard times.
Is there an hon. member who conscientiously believes that under the lopsided tariff schedules

Canada-United. States Trade Agreement
which now prevail we can achieve any measure of success in the development of Canadian industry, and thereby provide for the employment of our people? If there is such person I should like to know him.
It is a known fact that people of the United States, through a policy of protecting their own industry and giving employment to their own people at fair and equitable wage rates, have made that country one of the greatest nations of the world. Lincoln laid down the doctrine of government of the people, for the people and by the people. I believe we should adopt that policy in Canada. If we were to do so we should be taking an important step in the direction of lifting Canada out of the condition in which she is to-day, of placing ourselves back on the road to prosperity, of providing our youth with employment and our parents with the much desired and necessary purchasing power- which is so essential to the prosperity of the nation.
We have heard the argument advanced in the house that we must not antagonize the United States, and that in order to be assured of their friendliness, of necessity we must make trade agreements, with the knowledge that they will receive the lion's share. I do not believe for one moment that that is a sound argument. For over a hundred years we have lived as friendly nations, side by side, and I believe we shall continue to do so in the future. If we as a nation would make our trade treaties with the United States on the basis of a fair exchange of commodities, I believe that that government, instead of becoming antagonistic, would develop a greater respect for the government of this country and be more willing to cooperate than they were during the periods when the Hawley-Smoot and McCumber tariffs were applied against our producers.
I believe that this government stands condemned in the eyes of the business people of this country for having entered into a trade agreement without adequate knowledge of the results which might ultimately ensue. It is interesting to note that the concessions granted by the United States were considered carefully, and in no case was the slightest opportunity afforded to Canadian producers to obtain even a small percentage of the United States domestic market. Then as a further safeguard to the people of that country, the United States government has the privilege of applying quotas and regulations designed to restrict trade under any concession granted when it might interfere with home producers. As long as these tactics
are used against us, I believe we should adopt similar restrictions in connection with the concessions we grant.
If there is one thing needed in connection with the making of future agreements it is to have our tariff experts and those who make recommendations to the responsible ministers make a survey of the potential trade advantages to be gained and the possible disadvantages which might be sustained. This should be done in order that we may at least know where we are going when we consider an agreement of this kind in this house. We should know the amount of labour involved in producing any particular commodity. It is a known fact that for eight or ten months prior to the signing of this agreement the tariff committee of the United States government consulted with United States producers in order to learn what concessions might be advantageous and what might be disastrous in connection with any changes in the protection under which American industry was operating. The record of this government is entirely different. We not only made a pilgrimage to Washington and accepted what they offered but we made sacrifices in the markets of the United Kingdom, the extent of which will not be known for some time to come.
I have endeavoured to be as brief as possible and I think it will be found that I have kept well within my time limit, without asking for any extension.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution before the house asks our approval of the terms and provisions of a new Canada-United States trade agreement. This trade agreement replaces the agreement of 1935 and is now part of the tariff structure of this country. The 1935 agreement was supplanted before it had run to maturity, because of developments in the relations between Great Britain and the United States. These countries having expressed a desire to negotiate a reciprocal trade agreement, an important situation was created for Canada. Our government found it necessary to cooperate with our two greatest customers for the purpose of the extension and promotion of trade. To have refused would have certainly created a most unfavourable reaction which could not have been justified on any grounds. Under ordinary circumstances the government could have been required to carry out separate negotiations within the near future. The situation which was created really afforded an opportunity to Canada to negotiate a new immediate trade agreement with the United
1686	COMMONS
Canada-United. States Trade Agreement
States. That new trade agreement has been signed, with the result that our favourable trade relations with that country have been amplified and extended for another three years. I believe that this new arrangement will not only maintain Canada's trade position, but improve it considerably.
As far as our trade relations with Great Britain are concerned, certain amendments were made at her request. There is no doubt that certain concessions were granted but, on the other hand, there are compensations in the United States agreement which are more attractive to Canadian business generally. I know that the new agreement appeals to the people along the Atlantic coast and to the people in Queens-Lunenburg, the constituency which I have the honour to represent. These negotiations have placed Canada in harmony with her two greatest customers, the United Kingdom and our great neighbour to the south. The amendments made in the threeway agreement will no doubt justify in the minds of the British authorities a continuance without interruption of our present imperial trade relations. I think it was a splendid thing that these matters could be considered concurrently, and thus make provision for the immediate future. It produces a tariff stability which I believe is highly reassuring to business generally. To be constantly changing the tariff is disconcerting to business arrangements, and a measure of permanence is always greatly to be desired.
If we are to judge from the comments made in this house by hon. members of the Conservative party under the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), we must conclude that they are opposed to this agreement. I think we have here the line of demarcation between the policies of the two great parties in this country. The Liberal policy is one of extension of trade and promotion of goodwill. The Conservative party preach a doctrine of economic nationalism.

No, the route my hon. friends are travelling is this, that when every kind of fish is granted a reduction of duty, it is of no value in their eyes; the only thing that is of value in their eyes is the thing we did not get, and that is salt mackerel.
The reductions in duties on fish are very sweeping. In addition to what I have already mentioned there is a 50 per cent reduction on finnan haddie and smoked cod, hake, pollock, cusk and herring, 40 per cent on smoked salmon, 33 per cent on smoked fillets of cod, haddock, hake, pollock and cusk, of which over 3,500,000 pounds were shipped last year which means that nearly 10,000,000 pounds of round fish are caught. There is a 50 per cent reduction on halibut, salmon, swordfish, mackerel, shad, eels and sturgeon, as well as keeping free of duty for the life of the treaty such items as lobsters, scallops, oysters, clams, quahaugs and smelts, and a 50 per cent reduction on pickled and salted cod, haddock, hake, pollock and cusk. Last year the United States purchased from us approximately 25,000,000 pounds of these fish. This reduction also applies to the duty on pickled salmon and alewives, while there is a thirty-eight per cent reduction on split herring and a twenty-five per cent reduction on salted cod, haddock, hake, pollock and cusk when skinned and boned.

Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
Some people in Nova Scotia who are enthusiastic about their own particular business, as I suppose is to be expected, complain about the relative duty as between dry salted fish with over forty-three per cent of moisture and dry salted fish with less than forty-three per cent of moisture. Here is the story. Prior to this agreement the duty on cod containing not more than forty-three per cent of moisture was 1| cents, which meant $1.40 on each quintal of fish; and when containing over forty-three per cent of moisture the duty was three-quarters of a cent a pound or eighty-four cents on each quintal of fish, the difference being fifty-six cents. In the trade agreement the duty on fish containing not over forty-three per cent of moisture was reduced to five-eighths of a cent a pound, which amounts to seventy cents on a quintal of fish; on fish containing over forty-three per cent of moisture the duty was reduced to three-eighths of a cent a pound or forty-two cents a quintal, the difference being twenty-eight cents. So it will be seen that the agreement is an improvement in the interests of those marketing the drier fish. It would have been very nice to get a larger reduction, but in each case the maximum reduction of fifty per cent was made. It must not be forgotten that total imports into the United States of fish with over forty-three per cent of moisture had a market value of $2,008,136, of which Canada supplied $893,524 worth. The total value of imports of fish containing not more than forty-three per cent of moisture was $150,008, of which Canada supplied $77,659 worth.
In the Mackenzie-Zwicker report, the importance of keeping the price of fish low in the foreign market, so that it will be within the price range of mass consumption, is stressed. The fact is that there is a reduction of seventy cents a quintal in the duty on dried fish, while the price of these fish to the primary producer is quoted at $4.50 a quintal for large fish and S3.75 for medium fish, so it will be seen that the duty is quite a good percentage of the primary cost.
With regard to the competition of Newfoundland, it is true that we have that competition, and they seem to have an advantage with Labrador slop fish that are sent to the Porto Rico market. It may be that Canadian and Newfoundland interests should cooperate to bring about stability in the foreign market for salted fish, because Newfoundland is much the larger producer of salted cod fish.
By reason of the British agreement we have obtained a reduction on another fish, namely kippers, from three cents to two cents a
pound. The kipper is a popular fish, especially for breakfast. It will be recalled that the press, whether for the sake of advertising or as a matter of general interest, stated that President Roosevelt usually ate scrambled eggs for breakfast; but when Anthony Eden visited the United States, that handsome, stream-lined Englishman ate a kippered herring for his breakfast.
Fish is a highly perishable product; in the interests of the fishermen and the shippers I believe that with our market extended under this treaty, some provision should be made for the orderly marketing of this product, and I think this would be generally accepted as a benefit to all.
I should now like to say a word with regard to manufacturing.

speechtext: I do not desire to impose upon the time of the house. I should like to have said something about manufacturing and farming, but time will not permit. I think, however, I have said enough to convince the house that so far as the fishing industry is concerned, this trade agreement is the best achievement of any government in Canada for some years. I should like to compliment the government at this time, because when the 1935 agreement was negotiated we felt rather disappointed. Now, however, after a few years of industrious endeavour on the part of members from the maritime provinces, we find that one of the major items in this trade agreement provides that fish from the maritime provinces shall have freer access to the United States market, which for many kinds of fish is our natural market, near at hand and with a large consuming population.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman may
think and apparently his associates agree, that he can handle the case for the Conservatives by himself, as against the twenty-five Liberals. May I say to him that I have no reason for rising in my place in the House of Commons and criticizing the government, because everything it has done has met with my approval and that of my constituents. I can well understand that perhaps the hon. member feels he has some

apology to make to the people of the maritime provinces for the stand he has taken. I am sure if he recalls the year 1932, when one could buy in the county of Carleton a dozen eggs, a barrel of potatoes and a pound of butter for thirty-seven cents, he will not be so free to criticize at the present time. That seems to be enough on that score.
Perhaps at this stage it might not be a bad idea, after listening to the speeches which have been made, to consider exactly what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had in mind when he went to the United States to negotiate the trade treaty. I am sure if he had any particular part of Canada in mind, then surely that part must have been the maritime provinces. Undoubtedly his prime intention was to break down trade barriers. Any hon. member who looks impartially at the trade treaty will see that undoubtedly that was one of the objects the Prime Minister had in mind. He desired to arrange matters so as to permit goods to flow out of Canada into the United States, and from that country into Canada. He desired undoubtedly to give us an opportunity to get rid of our surplus goods. He desired to allow us to get in exchange those commodities we require. In addition to that, I have no doubt he wished to destroy those feelings of enmity and ill will which had grown up between Canada and the United States and between United States and Great Britain.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: There never was any ill will.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
As a final object I am quite sure he desired to draw the democracies of the world closer together in a bond of unity. Hon. members opposite may refer to the trade agreement as an effort towards economic appeasement, if they so desire. But call it what they may, I certainly believe, and I believe the people of Canada will agree, that was a worthy and desirable object.
There are certain things the treaty was not intended to do. May I say that I marvel at the faith and confidence which hon. members of the opposition have in the efficacy of the policies of the present government. There was no intention whatever in the minds of those who negotiated the treaty to put anything over the people of the United States. This was no horse-trading deal. Undoubtedly we desired that they should receive benefits, and that in return we should receive benefits. We had no objection to the people of the United States gaining something, and we expected that in return we would gain something. Certainly it was not the intention of

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
the Prime Minister to prevent United States goods from coming into this country. Above all things, never for one moment did it cross his mind that the trade treaty alone would end unemployment, start the wheels of industry to run, pay off the national debt, abolish all taxation, and fill the pockets of Canadians with money taken from the pockets of the people of the United States. Nor was it the belief of the Prime Minister that the trade treaty would make of Canada a Heaven on earth.

speechtext:
This is merely a step in the right direction, and it will remove the obstructions which have been damming up channels of trade and surrounding the nations of the world with Chinese walls. In other words, it was intended to break down tariffs.
I should like for a few moments to show the house what high tariffs have done to the maritime provinces. Certainly I do not have to argue in this fashion before the people of my own constituency, because they are well aware of the truth of what I am about to say. High tariffs have raised the prices of goods to consumers, for the benefit of industrial centres. That is a statement which is accepted as truth by the people in my constituency. The policy of high tariffs has undoubtedly created discontent in the minds of people, so far as the operation of the confederation of 1867 is concerned. They feel they have been discriminated against and that they, as consumers, have been sacrificed for the benefit of manufacturing centres. The belief has stirred up animosity between the maritime and the central provinces, and between west and east. I believe no person will deny that the high tariff policy has increased unemployment from approximately 100,000 persons to about a million and a half. By destroying trade it has brought the country to the verge of financial ruin. It has stirred up international ill will, and that ill will has extended even to England. It is well known by the people in my constituency that they always have hard times under Tory governments, but that under Liberal rule they always have better times.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Will the hon. member say that there are good times in his constituency to-day?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I will say they are infinitely better than they were when the Tory government was in power. I believe, if the hon. member is fair, he will admit the truth of what I said a few moments ago in connection with Carleton.
What are the arguments against the treaty? I have listened to this debate since it first began, and I am sure that the general public have reached the conclusion that the arguments against this trade treaty are based on the opinions of penny newspapers, nickel magazines and other one-man opinions; they are based on claptrap and balderdash. There has been but a single idea in mind-the personal aggrandizement of the writer. These arguments have been put forth apparently with the idea that if you throw a lot of mud, some of it will stick.
The hon. member for Royal referred to potatoes. I am surprised at his mention of potatoes in view of the unsavoury connection that vegetable has with his own party in the maritime provinces. He should have followed the example of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Patterson) and mentioned the additional 12,500,000 bushels of potatoes which will be allowed into the United States market by the increased quota. Our hon. friends have picked out single items to discuss and have not considered the treaty as a whole. I do not know how one can discover its benefits unless one considers it as a unit. The trouble is that the Tories can never get out of their own backyards. Several of them, when making speeches, got lost in their own apple orchards. I wonder why it is they can never take a national view? The irony of it is that they call their policy a national policy.
I support this treaty, first, because it fulfils the intentions for which it was created. Second, it undoubtedly benefits the fishermen by fixing free entry and gives three years of stability. Third, it helps the farmer to sell his potatoes, practically the only exportable farm crop in New Brunswick. Fourth, it helps in the export of lumber and lumber products. This treaty benefits the three basic industries of my own county, namely, farming, fishing and lumbering.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I were to choose a mediator to bring central and eastern Canada together, it certainly would not be the last speaker (Mr. Barry).
I have no apologies to offer for continuing the debate on the trade agreement with the United States, because it materially affects the jobs and the standard of living of thousands of industrial workers in my constituency. For the past four years many of these workers have been out of employment or have been reduced to working only two or three days a week because of the tremendous increase in imports from the United States and other foreign countries. There has been at
1694	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
least one result from this debate; the cattle quota has been increased. I have no doubt that when the debate is concluded we will see messengers being sent to the United States by this government in an effort to remedy the inequalities from which Canada is suffering because of this treaty.
I feel it is my duty to deal with this matter as a representative of the industrial constituency of Hamilton East. I think I should express what I believe to be the views of the people of my constituency with regard to this agreement, which the right lion. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said would effect a major reconstruction of the Canadian tariff. In the city of Hamilton, part of which I represent, there are about five hundred diversified industries, dealing with all forms of iron, steel, textiles, fibre, rubber, wood and food products. These industries employ some 33,000 persons, produce goods to the value of S185,-000,000 a year, and pay wages and salaries to the extent of $40,000,000 annually. This is purchasing power, about which some of our friends to my left are so eagerly inquiring.
Hamilton, situated in the heart of the famous Niagara fruit belt, provides a splendid consumers' market for the many hundreds of fruit, vegetable and dairy farmers who live in the surrounding districts. Hundreds of manufacturing firms are dependent upon the iron, steel and textile industries for the materials and supplies with which to manufacture their products. Hundreds of merchants, retailers, barbers, professional men, doctors and others are dependent upon the wages and salaries of these employees. Practically all of these industries are dependent for their existence upon a reasonable amount of tariff protection. That reasonable amount of tariff protection was considerably impaired by the trade treaty of 1935 with the United States, and considerable harm was done to our industries. By the trade treaty now before the house this reasonable measure of protection is further impaired. Our industries are being handicapped by the mass production competition of the United States, and the competition of low wages and standards of living which prevail in other favoured nations which are to receive the same benefits under this agreement as the United States, without their granting any concessions to Canada.
When the Prime Minister introduced the trade agreement to the house in 1936, he and other members of his government predicted that the increase in trade which would follow that agreement would bring untold benefits to Canada, would increase our revenues, would cure our taxation troubles, would solve our

unemployment problem and raise our standard of living. Those predictions of the Prime Minister were never realized. While it is true that some parts of the country received temporary benefits during the three years this treaty was in operation, the fact remains that the same problems of unemployment and taxation are with us. During that three year period Canada purchased some $320,000,000 worth of goods more than she sold to the United States-and in this figure I am not including gold. These were principally manufactured or partly manufactured goods, with a high content of labour.
When the Prime Minister introduced the present trade treaty into the house with his lengthy and somewhat political utterances, which covered some sixteen and a half pages of Hansard, he ignored the fact that his 1936 predictions had not been realized. He again-spoke enthusiastically, even aggressively, of the benefits which Canada would receive under the new treaty. He reiterated his belief in the policy of the Liberal party, that trade was the panacea for all our political and economic problems, that trade was the basis of industrial and commercial development, that what Canada needed was trade. Canada's need of trade was emphasized on the ground that trade means increased production, increased consumption, increased distribution, increased transportation, increased employment, an increase in the standard of living, and consequently increased prosperity.
On March 17, 1938, when the United States and Canadian governments announced the signing of the new trade agreements, both issued press releases describing the benefits received and the concessions made by each party. While the Canadian release contained a fairly accurate account of those benefits and concessions, there was a lack of detail and also a lack of frankness in dealing with some of the items, while the press release issued by the United States government gave a full and complete account of the agreement, indicated quite clearly how the United States government had protected its markets by quota restrictions and then went on to give reasons to substantiate the statement that the United States benefited a great deal more than Canada from the agreement.
During his address in this debate the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) placed on Hansard the opinions of representative people and of newspapers in support of the new trade agreement; but I noticed that the dates of those opinions and newspaper quotations were within one week of the issue of the press release, and for that reason I would not place too high a value upon them,

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
because I do not think sufficient time had elapsed to study the effects of the new agreement upon Canadian industry. It is only now that our manufacturers, working men, farmers and fruit and vegetable growers are beginning to experience the disastrous effects the treaty has had in Canada, and I venture to say that those whose opinions the minister quoted would, if given the opportunity, revise them even at this comparatively early date.
I also should like to place on Hansard some opinions on the trade agreement that have been expressed in the United States and Canada. First, I quote from an editorial in the Labour Leader, dated December 2, 1938:
So far as we can learn, the new treaty has not been favourably received by either the east or the west. Last week a university professor from western Canada made a statement to the effect that the west had again been sold down the river. In the same week the Ontario Vegetable Growers' Association condemned the treaty on the grounds that it would be more difficult to dispose of their crops in the home market while at the same time the Canadian manufacturers were protesting that the removal of the three per cent excise tax would penalize many industries. We also learn that communications have been pouring in to the finance department from manufacturers protesting the tax on raw- materials when the finished products have been relieved of taxation.
From the Financial Post I quote this:
Commercial printers were amazed, alarmed and perplexed when they learned the terms of the Canada-United States trade treaty which provides for free entry of printed matter when shipped into Canada in individual packages valued at not more than one dollar.
The Toronto Globe and Mail of February 1 last has this heading:
Japan textiles crowd Canada. A. 0. Dawson defines the position of the world's textiles as desperate.
It goes on to say:
Mr. Dawson pointed out in one product alone Canada has imported in the first half of 1938 twenty-five per cent of Japan's total exports.
In the Financial Post of November 26, 1938, I find this heading:
British Columbia lumbermen speculate on the effect of the trade treaty.
The article goes on to say:
British Columbia lumbermen say it is largely a matter of opinion whether the advantages given in the United States market will compensate for their sacrifice of British preference in United Kingdom.
Again the Financial Post says:
Lifting of three per cent import excise will effect cuts in duty up to five per cent.
Then from the Toronto Evening Telegram of November 18, 1938, I quote this:
Canada pays large price to open doors of trading between Britain and the United States. Yields wheat and apple preference for cattle benefits in United States.
The New York Times of November 18, 1938,
says:
Farmers benefit under trade pact. British treaty an advantage to corn, rice, hogs, apples and citrus fruit producers. At present American wheat sold abroad is marketed at prices below domestic levels and the government makes up losses by export subsidies. The wheat concessions should go far in helping the American wheat farmer to reestablish a profitable market in Great Britain. Experts predict a fifty per cent expansion in Britain purchases of lard. The agreement likewise substantially enlarges British import quotas on pork, hams, cured pork and other products.
The Buffalo Courier of November 18, 1938, contains the following front page headline:
Preferred rates on Canadian shipments removed-Canadian grain will flow once more through our port-Welcome news to the thousands of grain workers who have suffered from reduced working hours since 1932.
There is no doubt that the operation of the present agreement during the past two months has affected adversely the basic steel, iron and textile industries not only in the city of Hamilton but throughout Canada. This effect will be reflected in reduced revenue, reduced purchasing power, an increase in taxation, an increase in the number of unemployed and an increase in the number on relief. In the year ending December 31, 1938, there were 19,166 individuals on relief in Hamilton, and I attribute that principally to the imports of United States manufactured goods under the 1935 agreement and to the apprehension of employers of labour as to the terms of the present agreement.
When the present government in 1936 reduced the tariff on washing machines, the Apex washer was being manufactured in Montreal by the Robert Mitchell Company. This machine is now being imported direct from the United States. The ABC washer was also being made in Canada by the Northern Electric Company, and it is now being imported in large quantities from their United States factories. My experience and observation of various industries in Hamilton have been that when the Canadian tariff is reduced beyond what may be considered the reasonable amount of protection necessary, Canadian industries that have parent companies in the United States immediately stop making their products in Canada and import direct from their factories in the United States. A reasonable protection is the amount of protection necessary to allow our manufacturers to compete with the products of other manufacturers coming into our markets. Percentage means nothing; it is simply a matter of the amount of protection necessary to enable our industries to keep their men employed.
